= Round-trip engineering

*Round-trip engineering* is the ability to make changes to either a model or the code generated from it, with each
change propagating automatically to the other so that both artifacts stay consistent. It is the tightest possible
integration of xref:model-driven-development.adoc[*model-driven development*] and
xref:reverse-engineering.adoc[*reverse engineering*]. Forward engineering generates code from a model, and round-trip
engineering additionally reconstructs the model from changes made directly to the code, in both directions,
indefinitely.

In practice, the idea works well for toy examples but struggles once a system reaches any real complexity. Forward
generation, from a high-level model down to low-level code, is comparatively tractable, because it only requires
expanding a design decision into its implementation. The reverse direction is much harder. Recovering the
higher-level architectural intent behind a piece of source code usually depends on design decisions that were never
recorded anywhere machine-readable, and this cannot realistically be automated in the general case.

Tooling that claims full round-trip support tends to fall back to partial synchronization, flagging conflicts for a
human to resolve rather than merging both directions automatically.

The idea traces to the xref:case.adoc[*computer-aided software engineering (CASE)*] tools of the 1980s and 1990s, and
it resurfaces wherever a modeling notation and its generated code are both expected to be edited directly, such as in
some xref:model-driven-architecture.adoc[*model-driven architecture*] toolchains.
